newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. blocking contracts under oil deal - Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. blocking contracts under oil deal - Iraq.

text.p: Iraq said on Friday the United States was blocking contracts under its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations for political reasons.

The official Iraqi News Agency (INA), carrying a letter from Foreign Minister Mohammad Saeed al-Sahaf to U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, said objections raised by the U.S. representative at the Iraq sanctions committee to hold up the contracts were "coercive and illogical."

"The U.S. representative...impeded and delayed the implementation of the memorandum of understanding (oil deal) in the first 180 days for ill-intentioned political reasons against the Iraqi people," INA said, quoting Sahaf.

Under the first six-month deal which ended on June 7, Iraq exported oil worth $2 billion to buy urgent needs to alleviate the suffering of Iraqi people under U.N. trade sanctions since Baghdad invaded Kuwait in 1990.

The U.N. renewed the programme for another 180 days early this month but Iraq has not yet started the exports, also worth $2 billion. The government has not yet completed its food distribution plan for the second six months.

Sahaf said Iraq had submitted 669 contracts and only 409 passed the sanctions committee. "It (U.S. alone) held up 166 contracts...which has delayed the arrival of commodities to Iraq for five months."
Iraq started exporting oil for the first six months on December 10 last year.

Sahaf said the U.S. had not submitted any reason for holding up contracts. "This is not only coercion but represents disregard of the responsibilities and duties of (U.N.) Security Council members," he said.

Iraq and the U.N. are locked in a row over inspections by international arms experts. The U.N. Special Commission disarming Iraq under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire has accused Baghdad of interfering with its helicopter flights and barring its experts from visiting certain sites in the vicinity of the capital.
Sahaf made no mention of the latest obstructions by Iraq, saying his country was providing all means to help U.N. food monitors accomplish their duties properly.
"They (food monitors) enjoy freedom of movement to carry out their tasks and also enjoy U.N. immunities and privileges mentioned in the memorandum of understanding," Sahaf said.

Food supplies and other humanitarian goods arriving in Iraq under the oil deal have to be distributed under U.N. supervision. More than 120 U.N. food monitors supervise the distribution in the central and southern parts of Iraq and 20 more are stationed in the three Kurdish provinces in the north.
